title: Blowback
author: Troy Nahumko
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Wildfire_smoke_in_St._Catharines_Ontario_4-680x510.jpg)

Photograph Source: Gogerr - [CC BY-SA
4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)

The morning of June 27, 2021: Lytton, British Columbia, woke up and, without
realizing it, set a record it never knew it was in the running for. This is,
in the popular imagination, the country of igloos and toques and six unbroken
months of snow, a place where the postcard weather report is permanently set
to "bundle up", the last country on earth anyone would picture reaching for
sunscreen instead of a parka. By midday it had reached 46.6°C (115.9°F), a new
Canadian all-time high. Not to be outdone by itself, it broke that record the
next day: 47.9°C (118.2°F). And on June 29, still climbing, alone now on a
mountain no one else in the country's recorded history had ever stood on, it
reached 49.6°C — 121.3°F, hotter than has ever been recorded in Las Vegas, a
desert city built to expect exactly this kind of heat and mocked, that week,
by a rail-and-river town in the Fraser Canyon. Then, on June 30, as though
some tribunal of sky-gods had decided a village had no business reaching that
high, a wall of fire came down out of the hills and in under twenty minutes,
did what fire does. Lytton did not burn partway. Lytton, as a going concern, a
post office, a grocery store, a shift at the mill, simply stopped being a
sentence with a subject in it.

It was not an act of God. It was an act of atmospheric chemistry, and the
chemistry has a return address. A hotter atmosphere holds more moisture, which
means longer droughts between longer downpours, which means forests primed
like kindling between floods; heat domes that would once have been freak
occurrences now arrive with the punctuality of a subscription service.
Scientists, who continue to suffer from the professional defect of checking
whether things are true before saying them, attributed the 2021 heat dome,
without much hedging, to human-caused warming. The kind of warming that does
not accumulate evenly, that has a ledger, and the ledger has a name at the top
of it.

Since 1750, Lytton's neighbor to the south has pumped more carbon into the
atmosphere than any other nation on earth, something on the order of a quarter
of everything that has ever gone up, roughly double the historical share of
China, the country the world outsourced everything to, now shouldered with the
"world's biggest polluter" label because it finally out-produces America in a
single year's tally. Cumulatively, ounce for ounce, degree for degree, nobody
has done more to cook the boreal forest than the country now presenting Canada
with an invoice for the smoke. That is not incidental irony. That is the whole
joke, and it is not funny, and the only man in the joke is the one who cannot
locate himself in it.

Ninety-four percent of Canada's forest sits on Crown land: the public's…at
least on paper. The logging companies that cut it don't own it; they hold
tenure, a license good for a footprint that can sprawl past ten thousand
square kilometers (roughly 3,861 square miles), large enough that from a
distance a company starts to resemble a small kingdom. They take the timber
and leave the slash, the deadfall, the understory tinder that a healthy fire
regime would once have burned off in small, survivable doses before a century
of total suppression let it all pile up like a debt nobody was paying down.
The profit gets harvested. The risk stays behind. Crown land in name,
everyone's problem in fact, which is a tidy enough metaphor for the emissions
themselves: the benefit privatized for a century and a half, the bill now
arriving, itemized, on a whole continent's front porch.

The World Cup final offered the same lesson in miniature. The tournament
arrived preaching universality while behaving like a private members' club.
FIFA's president found time to invent a "Peace Prize" of his own and hang it
around the neck of the tournament's host, as though history were something one
could sponsor between television timeouts. When an American striker's red-card
suspension inconveniently threatened the home team’s chances, it somehow
dissolved after a phone call. The laws of football, like so many other laws,
turned out to be firm principles right up until they encountered sufficient
influence.

The borders proved equally flexible. A Somali referee was turned back despite
carrying a valid visa. An Iraqi player and his team's photographer spent hours
in detention. Moroccan supporters discovered that permission to enter had
become a revocable privilege rather than a guarantee. The bid documents had
promised the world open doors. The small print, as usual, specified that
openness was conditional.

Even football itself yielded. A game that has survived wars, dictatorships and
commercial television with its two uninterrupted forty-five-minute halves
intact was quietly re-engineered to accommodate ‘hydration breaks’ (read
commercials), extended halftime entertainment and the rhythms of an American
broadcast schedule. It is remarkable how often institutions discover that
their oldest principles were merely provisional once sufficient money arrives.

Then came the only guest no committee could credential.

The northern smoke did not require a visa. It could not be detained, deported
or persuaded to wait politely behind a barrier. It crossed the border with the
same indifference to sovereignty that carbon has always shown. Molecules,
unlike politicians, have never mistaken a customs booth for a law of nature.
They followed the wind south, carrying with them a simple reminder that the
atmosphere remains stubbornly unimpressed by passports, tariffs or threats.
There was something almost poetic about it: the one arrival no wall could stop
drifting into the showcase event of an administration determined to
demonstrate that walls still worked.

Like salmon, it was only doing what it has always done. It was going home.

So the commander in chief did the only thing he knows how to do when the world
declines to cooperate with his sense of how it ought to behave: he blamed
someone else. He called Canada's fire season "willful negligence," accused
Ottawa of failing at "basic Forest Management and Debris Removal," and
announced that the cost of America's bad air would be added to the tariffs
Canada already pays, this, while nearly nine hundred wildfires burned across
Canada, and while a lightning-sparked outbreak of its own burned seventeen
fires through northern Minnesota that week, several of which crossed the
border and kept burning on the Canadian side. Ontario's premier, sounding less
like a diplomat than a man just tired, asked the country pricing the smoke to
send help instead of a bill. Firefighters, not fees. Water bombers, not
warnings. It is the reasoning of an arsonist suing the firefighters for
arriving too late.

There is an old imperial superstition that sees consequences as things that
happen in far away places. Wars happen abroad. Coups happen abroad. Famines
happen abroad. Refugees arrive from abroad. Carbon, however, has always been
embarrassingly provincial. It insists on coming home, whether you believe in
climate change or not. It drifts back across the frontier carrying no
ideology, no flag and no opinion about who started the fire. It merely
delivers the invoice.

Americans have long preferred to imagine blowback as a foreign language. It
came home from Kabul wearing boots stamped "Made in the U.S.A." It crossed the
Rio Grande speaking the dialect of decades spent backing dictators who were
dependable only in their appetite for power and American approval. Now it
arrives as smoke, carrying no ideology at all, only chemistry. It is coming
home now in the form of a specter that no longer has a shape, a fire season
that keeps breaking its own record, and a sky over New Jersey that FIFA has to
"monitor closely" before letting eighty thousand people breathe it through a
World Cup final.

Canada is the canary, and the coalmine is the one mostly built on the American
side of the line. Most climate catastrophes, hurricanes aside, carry the mercy
of distance for the United States: a drowned delta somewhere else, a burning
hillside where they don’t speak English, sad enough to acknowledge, far enough
to file away. This one arrived with every breath you take. It shut Broadway
marquees behind a curtain of haze and put free masks in a mayor's hands. And
on Thursday it reached into Central Park, where Mavis Staples, eighty-six
years old, a woman who marched with Dr. King and has spent eight decades
singing this country's conscience back to it one gospel chord at a time, was
silenced. Not by a permit denied, not by a network that grew tired of her, not
by white Christian nationalist threats, but by the air itself, made
unbreathable by the very ideology her whole career has stood against. The
conscience got canceled by the thing it kept warning everyone about.

That is the accounting nobody sends an invoice for. Two hundred and seventy-
five years of treating the atmosphere as a place to dump the cost of not
caring, and the bill arrives anyway, itemized in ash, delivered by a wind that
was never going to stop and ask permission. You can put a wall on a river. You
can put a fence across a desert. You cannot tariff the sky, and if you could,
the largest debtor in that particular ledger has never once, since 1750, been
Canada.
